title: The AI sell-off now has Taiwan taking emergency steps to calm its chip-heavy market
excerpt: Taiwan's financial regulators said Saturday it was limiting short selling after its main trading index fell 17.5% in five days.
content_html:
By Truman Dickerson

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-21T22:02:52.150Z

Financial regulators in Taiwan said they would limit short selling in local markets effective Monday, a move that could further rattle investors during an intense tech stock sell-off.

In a statement on Saturday, Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission said it was taking the action "in response to the recent significant fluctuations in the Taiwan stock market."

Taiwan's main trading index, which is heavily weighted toward semiconductor stocks, fell 17.5% over the last five trading days.

In US markets, the S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory on Friday, meaning they had fallen at least 10% from recent highs.

Some market pros have pointed to the week's stock market carnage to predict that the AI trade is at a turning point, possibly on its last legs as a host of headwinds reshape the outlook.

Michael Burry, the investor made famous by "The Big Short," reminded investors on Thursday that he's been sounding the alarm about chip makers and neoclouds for some time now.

"Coreweave, Nebius, Nvidia, semis, I tried to warn you all," he wrote on X. "I didn't say short. But I provided the information one would need to sell."

Taiwanese regulators said the limits comprised "a complete ban on short selling below the closing price."

"This does not apply to short selling and borrowing by securities firms and futures companies for hedging purposes," their statement said.

The limits on short-selling would hobble investors looking to hedge. To raise cash, they might sell their long positions.

In 2008, the US Securities and Exchange Commission temporarily banned short selling for a slew of financial stocks during the collapse of the housing market.

The intervention largely failed to ease the decline. Then SEC Chairman Christopher Cox said in a press release announcing the measure that it "would not be necessary in a well-functioning market."
